newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. auto group frets over S.Korea car capacity.
newsitem.headline: U.S. auto group frets over S.Korea car capacity.

text.p: South Korea is investing in auto production capacity in emerging markets at levels that defied financial logic, a U.S. auto manufacturers' representative said on Wednesday.

"We find that Korean automakers are very aggressive in overseas markets, particularly in growth markets of Eastern Europe, Latin America and Southeast Asia," said Andrew Card, president of the American Automobile Manufacturers' Association.
"Not only are exports up from Korea, but Korean companies continue to invest in these markets at levels that defy financial logic," he said.
He said "some observers" questioned whether South Korean automakers' overseas investments were being taken in line with internationally accepted trade and investment practices.
The combined annual capacity of South Korea's three leading car makers is about 4.2 million vehicles and is scheduled to top six million by 2000.
All three have invested in overseas production capacity, but Daewoo Motor Co Ltd has been most aggressive.
Their home sales, meanwhile, were about 1.6 million vehicles last year.
Card said the current crisis facing Kia Motors Corp could be "advance warning that Korea's huge expansion in the context of global over-capacity carries some big risks for the Korean auto industry."

South Korean banks stepped in on Tuesday to rescue the eighth-ranked Kia Group whose flagship car unit was hit by slumping home sales and heated competition from Daewoo. Analysts said Kia would likely be dismantled and sold off next year.
Camille Blum, secretary general of the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association, said South Korea's markets remained closed to imports even though it was increasing its exports.
"While imports face limits in this market, production by Korea's automakers continues to increase and exports, in particular, are up," Blum said.
"Currently Korea exports over 40 percent of its production, with even more capacity scheduled to come on line over the next several years."
Blum and Card were in Seoul to discuss concerns about South Korea's closed car market with officials from various government agencies and automotive groups.
The South Korean government should be more "pro-active" in informing consumers that it is acceptable to buy imported cars, Blum said.

South Korea's vehicle imports reached 10,315 units last year, which amounts to 0.62 percent of the market. Blum said sales of imported vehicles slipped 5.12 percent to 4,707 units in the first six months of this year.
